title: How to Plan for Retirement if You Don’t Want to Rely on Social Security
content:
Many younger workers are skeptical that Social Security will exist in its current form by the time they retire. While total insolvency is unlikely, benefit cuts or means-testing are possible political outcomes. Planning for a retirement with $0 in Social Security benefits is the ultimate stress test. If you can build a plan that works without the government, any benefits you do receive become 'Bonus Money' for luxury travel or charity. This guide outlines the aggressive savings metrics required to self-fund 100% of your future.

Key Takeaways

  • The Replacement Gap: Social Security replaces ~40% of income for average earners. Without it, your personal portfolio must cover 100% of your expenses. This requires a nest egg roughly 30-40% larger than standard guidelines.
  • Higher Savings Rate: To hit the larger target, the standard 'Save 15%' advice fails. You likely need to save 20-25% of gross income starting in your 20s or 30s.
  • Conservative Withdrawal: Without a guaranteed income floor (Social Security annuity), you bear all longevity risk. A 3.5% withdrawal rate is safer than 4% when you have no safety net.
  • Health Insurance Factor: Medicare faces similar funding challenges. A 'Zero-Gov' plan should also include a robust HSA balance to self-fund healthcare premiums if necessary.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The Social Security Trust Fund is projected to deplete reserves in the mid-2030s, triggering an automatic ~20% benefit cut unless Congress acts. Planning for $0 is a hedge against political deadlock.

The Self-Funded Calculator

Scenario: You spend $60,000/year. Goal: Age 65.

Standard Plan (With Social Security)

  • Spending: $60,000.
  • Social Security: -$30,000.
  • Portfolio Need: $30,000.
  • Nest Egg (25x): $750,000.

Zero-Gov Plan (Self-Funded)

  • Spending: $60,000.
  • Social Security: $0.
  • Portfolio Need: $60,000.
  • Nest Egg (25x): $1.5 Million.

The Cost of Skepticism: You must save double the amount ($1.5M vs $750k). To achieve this, you must double your monthly savings contribution or work ~7 years longer.

How to Hit the Higher Number

  1. Max 401(k) + IRA: You need to fill both buckets ($23k + $7k). $30k/year invested at 7% hits $1.5M in ~22 years. It is achievable for high earners.
  2. Rental Income: Create your own Social Security. Buying 2 rental properties that generate $1,500/mo net income replaces the government check with a private asset.
  3. Tax Diversification: If tax rates rise to fund Social Security, you want Roth assets. Having tax-free income protects you from the government solving its debt problem with your wallet.
  4. The 'Bonus' Mindset: If Social Security does pay out, you will be rich. You can upgrade from Economy to First Class. Plan for survival; hope for luxury.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it realistic to expect $0?

Probably not. It is a 'Worst Case' scenario. Even if benefits are cut 25%, you still get 75%. But planning for $0 makes you antifragile.

Should I opt out of paying taxes?

You can't. FICA taxes are mandatory. Consider them a charitable donation to current retirees, not an investment in your future.

Does this change my asset allocation?

Yes. Without the 'Bond-like' safety of Social Security, your personal portfolio needs more fixed income (Bonds/Annuities) to create a reliable floor.
